title: To me, fair friend
short: An anniversary sonnet: three years have passed since the poet first saw the friend, who seems unchanged.
body: The poem marks three years since the first meeting and asserts that, to the poet's eye, the friend has not aged. 'To me' immediately qualifies the claim: it is the lover's perception. Biographical critics have used the 'three years' to try to date the sequence, but many editors treat the figure as a poetic convention rather than a record, and the poem itself casts doubt on the reliability of the lover's eye.

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (New Haven: Yale UP, 1977; rev. 2000), commentary on the line
John Kerrigan, ed., The Sonnets and A Lover's Complaint (Penguin, 1986), commentary
'Sonnet 104', Wikipedia (summary of critical readings)

title: your eye I ey'd
short: A deliberate repetition of word and verb (polyptoton): the first meeting of eyes.
body: The repetition of 'eye' as noun and verb (polyptoton) makes the first meeting an exchange of looks, the traditional origin of love in Petrarchan poetry, where love enters through the eyes. The play also anticipates 'mine eye may be deceiv'd' in line 12: the organ that began the love is the one whose judgment is questioned. Elizabethan readers would know the doctrine that love is born in the eyes, as in Shakespeare's song 'Tell me where is fancy bred' (The Merchant of Venice 3.2).

sources.cite: Stephen Booth, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets (New Haven: Yale UP, 1977; rev. 2000), commentary on the line

title: Three winters ... three summers ... three springs
short: The triple cycle of seasons enumerates three years with rhetorical repetition across the quatrain boundary.
body: The second quatrain counts the years through the seasons: three winters have shaken off three summers' leaves, three springs turned to autumn, three Aprils burnt into Junes. The syntax runs on from line 3 ('Three winters cold, / Have from the forests shook') across the quatrain break. 'Pride' means splendour, the summer foliage. The order is irregular (winter, summer, spring, autumn, April, June), perhaps to suggest the blur of passing time. The rhetorical figure of repeated 'three' is anaphora.

title: In process of the seasons
short: In the course or progression of the seasons.
body: 'Process' here means the onward course of time. The phrase sounds legal as well as natural, as in the 'process' of law, but its main sense is the steady progression that the poem fears. 'Which yet are green' (line 8) means the friend is still youthful, with a contrast between green youth and the burnt Junes and yellow autumns. The word thus quietly joins the friend's unchanging face to the very movement of time that will alter it, a tension the third quatrain makes explicit.

title: like a dial-hand
short: Beauty moves imperceptibly away like the hand of a clock or sundial; 'dial' is pronounced as two syllables.
body: A 'dial-hand' is the pointer on a clock or the shadow on a sundial, whose movement cannot be seen. Beauty 'steals' from the figure in the same way. Booth notes that the metre requires 'dial' to be two syllables. The dial is a recurrent emblem of time in the sonnets (Sonnets 77, 'Thy dial how thy precious minutes waste'). The image overturns the opening confidence: the friend may be changing without the poet perceiving it.

title: Steal from his figure
short: Move away from its numeral on the dial, and also steal from the friend's beautiful form ('figure').
body: 'His' means 'its' (the usual Elizabethan neuter possessive). The dial-hand 'steals' (moves stealthily) from its 'figure', the number on the dial; at the same time beauty steals away from the friend's figure, or shape. 'No pace perceiv'd' means no step being seen. The double sense makes clock and face the same object. Booth's commentary shows how the sonnets often make one image serve two objects in this way. The thief-like motion recalls 'Time's thievish progress' in Sonnet 77.

title: mine eye may be deceiv'd
short: The lover admits his perception may be false: what seems to stand still is really moving.
body: The admission undermines the opening line. The friend's 'hue' (appearance, complexion), which 'methinks' still stands, has motion. The sonnets repeatedly question the lover's eye (compare Sonnets 113, 137, 148), and this poem dramatises the gap between perception and reality. It also prepares the couplet's paradoxical consolation. The sonnet's turn at line 9 ('Ah! yet') marks the point where certainty yields to doubt; the poem's claim of permanence is undercut by its own evidence. The admission is followed by a defensive address to posterity.

title: thou age unbred
short: Future generations, not yet born, are addressed directly with the poem's verdict.
body: 'Age unbred' is the age not yet begotten, posterity. The address 'hear this' (with a mid-line reversal of stress) turns the poem from the friend to future readers, as the sequence elsewhere turns to posterity to guarantee the friend's fame (Sonnets 18, 55). Here the message is that the perfect beauty those future ages might hope for has already passed.

title: Ere you were born was beauty's summer dead
short: Before future ages are born, beauty's summer, the friend in his prime, will be dead: an extravagant compliment.
body: The couplet's hyperbole makes the friend the absolute standard of beauty: whatever the future sees, its 'summer' died before it was born. The line recalls the seasonal imagery of the quatrains and the famous comparison to 'a summer's day' (Sonnet 18). Some readers find the compliment consoling, others hear in it a concession that the friend too will age and die.
